claim: Recent reconstructions by electron tomography (Kiewisz et al., 2022) captured the positions and configurations of every MT in human mitotic spindles.
source: Recent reconstructions by electron tomography (Kiewisz et al., 2022) captured the positions and configurations of every MT in human mitotic spindles, revealing that roughly half the KMTs in these spindles do not reach the pole.
evidence: Cites Kiewisz et al., 2022 as the source of electron tomography reconstructions

claim: Roughly half the KMTs in human mitotic spindles do not reach the pole.
source: Recent reconstructions by electron tomography (Kiewisz et al., 2022) captured the positions and configurations of every MT in human mitotic spindles, revealing that roughly half the KMTs in these spindles do not reach the pole.
evidence: Based on electron tomography data from Kiewisz et al., 2022

claim: In metaphase, KMTs grow away from the kinetochores along well-defined trajectories.
source: Our results indicate that in metaphase, KMTs grow away from the kinetochores along well-defined trajectories, with the speed of the KMT minus ends continually decreasing as the minus ends approach the pole, implying that longer KMTs grow more slowly than shorter KMTs.
evidence: Supported by photoconversion experiments and analysis of electron tomography data

claim: The speed of the KMT minus ends continually decreases as the minus ends approach the pole.
source: Our results indicate that in metaphase, KMTs grow away from the kinetochores along well-defined trajectories, with the speed of the KMT minus ends continually decreasing as the minus ends approach the pole, implying that longer KMTs grow more slowly than shorter KMTs.
evidence: Measured through photoconversion experiments showing spatially varying speeds

claim: Longer KMTs grow more slowly than shorter KMTs.
source: Our results indicate that in metaphase, KMTs grow away from the kinetochores along well-defined trajectories, with the speed of the KMT minus ends continually decreasing as the minus ends approach the pole, implying that longer KMTs grow more slowly than shorter KMTs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that KMT minus end speed decreases as they approach the pole

claim: The locations of KMT minus ends and the turnover and movements of tubulin in KMTs are consistent with models in which KMTs predominately nucleate de novo at kinetochores in metaphase.
source: The locations of KMT minus ends, and the turnover and movements of tubulin in KMTs, are consistent with models in which KMTs predominately nucleate de novo at kinetochores in metaphase and are inconsistent with substantial numbers of non-KMTs being recruited to the kinetochore in metaphase.
evidence: Based on comparison of electron tomography data, photoconversion experiments, and mathematical modeling

claim: The locations of KMT minus ends and the turnover and movements of tubulin in KMTs are inconsistent with substantial numbers of non-KMTs being recruited to the kinetochore in metaphase.
source: The locations of KMT minus ends, and the turnover and movements of tubulin in KMTs, are consistent with models in which KMTs predominately nucleate de novo at kinetochores in metaphase and are inconsistent with substantial numbers of non-KMTs being recruited to the kinetochore in metaphase.
evidence: Based on comparison of electron tomography data, photoconversion experiments, and mathematical modeling

claim: A spindle composed of microtubules (MTs) and associated proteins assembles and segregates the chromosomes to the daughter cells during eukaryotic cell division.
source: When eukaryotic cells divide, a spindle composed of microtubules (MTs) and associated proteins assembles and segregates the chromosomes to the daughter cells (Strasburger, 1880; McIntosh et al., 2012; Heald and Khodjakov, 2015; Petry, 2016; Prosser and Pelletier, 2017, Oriola et al., 2018, O'Toole et al., 2020, Anjur-Dietrich et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature

claim: A macromolecular protein complex called the kinetochore binds each sister chromatid to MTs in the spindle.
source: A macromolecular protein complex called the kinetochore binds each sister chromatid to MTs in the spindle thereby bi-orienting the two sisters to ensure they segregate to opposite daughter cells (McDonald et al., 1992; McEwen et al., 1997; Maiato et al., 2004a; Yoo et al., 2018, Monda and Cheeseman, 2018; Rieder, 1982; Maiato et al., 2004b, Musacchio and Desai, 2017, Pesenti, 2018; Monda and Cheeseman, 2018; DeLuca et al., 2011; Redemann et al., 2017; Long et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature

claim: The kinetochore bi-orients the two sister chromatids to ensure they segregate to opposite daughter cells.
source: A macromolecular protein complex called the kinetochore binds each sister chromatid to MTs in the spindle thereby bi-orienting the two sisters to ensure they segregate to opposite daughter cells (McDonald et al., 1992; McEwen et al., 1997; Maiato et al., 2004a; Yoo et al., 2018, Monda and Cheeseman, 2018; Rieder, 1982; Maiato et al., 2004b, Musacchio and Desai, 2017, Pesenti, 2018; Monda and Cheeseman, 2018; DeLuca et al., 2011; Redemann et al., 2017; Long et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature

claim: Any MT whose plus end is embedded in the kinetochore is referred to as a kinetochore microtubule (KMT).
source: Any MT whose plus end is embedded in the kinetochore is referred to as a kinetochore microtubule (KMT) and the collection of all KMTs associated with an individual kinetochore is called a kinetochore-fiber (K-Fiber).
evidence: Definition provided in the manuscript

claim: The collection of all KMTs associated with an individual kinetochore is called a kinetochore-fiber (K-Fiber).
source: Any MT whose plus end is embedded in the kinetochore is referred to as a kinetochore microtubule (KMT) and the collection of all KMTs associated with an individual kinetochore is called a kinetochore-fiber (K-Fiber).
evidence: Definition provided in the manuscript

claim: The kinetochore-microtubule interaction stabilizes KMTs.
source: The kinetochore-microtubule interaction stabilizes KMTs and generates tension across the sister chromatid pair (Brinkley and Cartwright, 1975; Gorbsky and Borisy, 1989; Nicklas and Ward, 1994; Bakhoum et al., 2009; DeLuca et al., 2006; Cheeseman et al., 2006; Tanaka and Desai, 2008; Akiyoshi et al., 2010; Kabeche and Compton, 2013; Cheerambathur et al., 2017; Monda and Cheeseman, 2018; Steblyanko et al., 2020; Warren et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature

claim: The kinetochore-microtubule interaction generates tension across the sister chromatid pair.
source: The kinetochore-microtubule interaction stabilizes KMTs and generates tension across the sister chromatid pair (Brinkley and Cartwright, 1975; Gorbsky and Borisy, 1989; Nicklas and Ward, 1994; Bakhoum et al., 2009; DeLuca et al., 2006; Cheeseman et al., 2006; Tanaka and Desai, 2008; Akiyoshi et al., 2010; Kabeche and Compton, 2013; Cheerambathur et al., 2017; Monda and Cheeseman, 2018; Steblyanko et al., 2020; Warren et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature

claim: Modulation of the kinetochore-MT interaction is thought to be important in correcting mitotic errors.
source: Modulation of the kinetochore-MT interaction is thought to be important in correcting mitotic errors (DeLuca et al., 2011; Godek et al., 2015; Funabiki, 2019; Long et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature

claim: Kinetochore-MT binding is central to normal mitotic progression and correctly segregating sister chromatids to opposite daughter cells.
source: Kinetochore-MT binding is thus central to normal mitotic progression and correctly segregating sister chromatids to opposite daughter cells (Cimini et al., 2001; Chiang et al., 2010; Auckland and McAinsh, 2015; Lampson and Grishchuk, 2017; Dudka et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature

claim: Chromosome segregation errors are implicated in a host of diseases ranging from cancer to development disorders such as Downs' and Turners' Syndromes.
source: Chromosome segregation errors are implicated in a host of diseases ranging from cancer to development disorders such as Downs' and Turners' Syndromes (Touati and Wassmann, 2016; Compton, 2017, Jo et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature

claim: In metaphase, KMTs turnover with a half-life of ~2.5min.
source: In metaphase, KMTs turnover with a half-life of ~2.5min, so the KMTs that originally attached during initial spindle assembly in early prometaphase have long since detached from the kinetochore and been replaced by freshly recruited KMTs over the ~25min from nuclear envelope breakdown to anaphase.
evidence: Based on photoconversion experiments measuring KMT turnover

claim: The number of KMTs remains relatively constant over the course of mitosis.
source: The number of KMTs remains relatively constant over the course of mitosis (McEwen et al., 1997; McEwen et al., 1998), so new KMTs must be continually recruited to kinetochores throughout metaphase to replace the detaching KMTs.
evidence: Supported by citations to McEwen et al. studies

claim: New KMTs must be continually recruited to kinetochores throughout metaphase to replace the detaching KMTs.
source: The number of KMTs remains relatively constant over the course of mitosis (McEwen et al., 1997; McEwen et al., 1998), so new KMTs must be continually recruited to kinetochores throughout metaphase to replace the detaching KMTs.
evidence: Logical inference from constant KMT number and turnover

claim: Kinetochores are capable of both nucleating KMTs de novo and capturing existing non-KMTs.
source: Prior experiments have established that kinetochores are capable of both nucleating KMTs de novo and capturing exiting non-KMTs (Telzer et al., 1975; ; Mitchison and Kirschner, 1985a; Mitchison and Kirschner, 1985b, Mitchison and Kirschner, 1986, Huitorel and Kirschner, 1988; Heald and Khodjakov, 2015; LaFountain and Oldenbourg, 2014; Petry, 2016; Sikirzhytski et al., 2018; David et al., 2019; Renda and Khodjakov, 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior experimental work

claim: Once attached, the plus-ends of KMTs can polymerize and depolymerize while remaining attached to the kinetochore, leading to a net flux of tubulin through the K-Fiber from the kinetochore toward the spindle pole.
source: Once attached, the plus-ends of KMTs can polymerize and depolymerize while remaining attached to the kinetochore, leading to a net flux of tubulin through the K-Fiber from the kinetochore toward the spindle pole (Mitchison and Kirschner, 1985a, Mitchison, 1989; Rieder and Alexander, 1990; Mitchison and Salmon, 1992; Zhai et al., 1995; Waters et al., 1996; Khodjakov et al., 2003; Gadde and Heald, 2004; McIntosh et al., 2012; Steblyanko et al., 2020; DeLuca et al., 2011; Elting et al., 2014; Elting et al., 2017, Neahring et al., 2021; Risteski et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior experimental work

claim: The regulation of KMT detachments is thought to be important for correcting improper attachments and ensuring accurate chromosome segregation.
source: Finally, when KMTs detach from the kinetochore, they become non-KMTs by definition. The regulation of KMT detachments is thought to be important for correcting improper attachments and ensuring accurate chromosome segregation (Tanaka et al., 2002; Bakhoum et al., 2009, DeLuca et al., 2011; Godek et al., 2015; Krenn and Musacchio, 2015; Lampson and Grishchuk, 2017; Funabiki, 2019; Long et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature

claim: KMT detachments typically occur with a time scale of ~2.5min in metaphase in human mitotic cells.
source: KMT detachments typically occur with a time scale of ~2.5min in metaphase in human mitotic cells (Kabeche and Compton, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kabeche and Compton, 2013

claim: Serial-section electron tomography was used to reconstruct the locations, lengths, and configurations of MTs in metaphase spindles in HeLa cells.
source: In a companion paper, we used serial-section electron tomography to reconstruct the locations, lengths, and configurations of MTs in metaphase spindles in HeLa cells (Kiewisz et al., 2022).
evidence: Cites Kiewisz et al., 2022 as companion paper

claim: Whole spindle reconstructions can unambiguously identify which MTs are bound to the kinetochore and measure their lengths.
source: These whole spindle reconstructions can unambiguously identify which MTs are bound to the kinetochore and measure their lengths, providing a remarkable new tool for the study of KMTs.
evidence: Based on the capabilities of electron tomography reconstructions

claim: Only ~50% of KMTs have their minus ends at spindle poles.
source: The electron tomography reconstructions revealed that only ~50% of KMTs have their minus ends at spindle poles.
evidence: Based on analysis of electron tomography data

claim: While KMT stability does not spatially vary, their speed is greatest in the middle of the spindle and continually decreases closer to poles.
source: We used photoconversion experiments to measure the dynamics of KMTs, which revealed that while their stability does not spatially vary, their speed is greatest in the middle of the spindle and continually decreases closer to poles.
evidence: Based on photoconversion experiments

claim: The orientations of MTs throughout the spindle can be quantitively explained by an active liquid crystal theory in which the mutual interactions between MTs cause them to locally align with each other.
source: We next show that the orientations of MTs throughout the spindle, measured by electron tomography and polarized light microscopy, can be quantitively explained by an active liquid crystal theory in which the mutual interactions between MTs cause them to locally align with each other.
evidence: Based on comparison of experimental measurements with theoretical predictions

claim: KMTs tend to move along well-defined trajectories in the spindle.
source: This argues that KMTs tend to move along well-defined trajectories in the spindle.
evidence: Inferred from the agreement between MT orientations and active liquid crystal theory

claim: The distribution of KMT minus ends along trajectories is only consistent with the motion and turnover of KMTs if KMTs predominately nucleate at kinetochores.
source: We show that the distribution of KMT minus ends along these trajectories (measured by electron tomography) is only consistent with the motion and turnover of KMTs (measured by photoconversion) if KMTs predominately nucleate at kinetochores.
evidence: Based on comparison of electron tomography data, photoconversion experiments, and mathematical modeling

claim: Metaphase KMTs nucleate at the kinetochore and grow towards the spindle pole along defined trajectories.
source: Taken together, these results lead us to construct a model in which metaphase KMTs nucleate at the kinetochore and grow towards the spindle pole along defined trajectories.
evidence: Based on integration of electron tomography, photoconversion, and modeling results

claim: The KMT minus ends slow down as they approach the pole.
source: The KMT minus ends slow down as they approach the pole.
evidence: Based on photoconversion experiments showing spatially varying speeds

claim: Since the flux of tubulin is constant throughout a single KMT at any given moment in time, the minus end slowdown is coupled to a decrease in the polymerization rate at the KMT plus end.
source: Since the flux of tubulin is constant throughout a single KMT at any given moment in time, the minus end slowdown is coupled to a decrease in the polymerization rate at the KMT plus end.
evidence: Logical inference from conservation of tubulin flux

claim: KMTs detach from the kinetochore at a constant rate, independent of the minus end position.
source: KMTs detach from the kinetochore at a constant rate, independent of the minus end position.
evidence: Based on photoconversion experiments showing uniform KMT turnover

claim: KMTs are defined as MTs with one end near a kinetochore in the reconstructions.
source: We defined KMTs as MTs with one end near a kinetochore in the reconstructions and assigned the plus end to the end at the kinetochore and the minus end to the opposite end of the MT (Figure 1A).
evidence: Definition used in the analysis of electron tomography data

claim: Approximately 51% of KMT minus ends are more than 1.7μm away from the pole.
source: KMT minus ends are located throughout the spindle, with approximately 51% of them more than 1.7μm away from the pole, as found in Kiewisz et al., 2022 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Based on analysis of electron tomography data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The location of the pole was defined as the center of the mother centriole.
source: We defined the location of the pole as the center of the mother centriole.
evidence: Definition used in the analysis

claim: KMT minus ends are distributed throughout individual K-Fibers.
source: KMT minus ends are distributed throughout individual K-Fibers (Figure 1C), indicating that the processes that lead to a broad distribution of KMT minus end locations can occur at the level of individual kinetochores.
evidence: Based on analysis of electron tomography data shown in Figure 1C

claim: The processes that lead to a broad distribution of KMT minus end locations can occur at the level of individual kinetochores.
source: KMT minus ends are distributed throughout individual K-Fibers (Figure 1C), indicating that the processes that lead to a broad distribution of KMT minus end locations can occur at the level of individual kinetochores.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that KMT minus ends are distributed throughout individual K-Fibers

claim: After photoactivating a line of tubulin in the spindle, the converted tubulin moves poleward and fades over time.
source: After photoactivating a line of tubulin in the spindle, the converted tubulin moves poleward and fades over time (Figure 2A; Mitchison, 1989; DeLuca, 2010; Kabeche and Compton, 2013; Fürthauer et al., 2019; Steblyanko et al., 2020).
evidence: Based on photoactivation experiments shown in Figure 2A and supported by citations

claim: The two-photon photoactivation produced a narrow line in the z-direction perpendicular to the imaging plane (σ=1.0 ± 0.1µm).
source: The two-photon photoactivation produced a narrow line in the z-direction perpendicular to the imaging plane (σ=1.0 ± 0.1µm), so the contribution of out of focus photoactivated tubulin entering the imaging plane is minimal (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The contribution of out of focus photoactivated tubulin entering the imaging plane is minimal.
source: The two-photon photoactivation produced a narrow line in the z-direction perpendicular to the imaging plane (σ=1.0 ± 0.1µm), so the contribution of out of focus photoactivated tubulin entering the imaging plane is minimal (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inferred from the narrow z-profile of photoactivation

claim: The tubulin turnover is well-fit by a dual-exponential decay.
source: Since the tubulin turnover is well-fit by a dual-exponential decay, it suggests that there are two subpopulations of MTs with different stabilities in the spindle, as previously argued for many model systems (Brinkley and Cartwright, 1975; Salmon et al., 1976; Lambert and Bajer, 1977, Rieder and Bajer, 1977; Rieder, 1981; Cassimeris et al., 1990; DeLuca, 2010).
evidence: Based on fitting photoconversion data to dual-exponential decay

claim: There are two subpopulations of MTs with different stabilities in the spindle.
source: Since the tubulin turnover is well-fit by a dual-exponential decay, it suggests that there are two subpopulations of MTs with different stabilities in the spindle, as previously argued for many model systems (Brinkley and Cartwright, 1975; Salmon et al., 1976; Lambert and Bajer, 1977, Rieder and Bajer, 1977; Rieder, 1981; Cassimeris et al., 1990; DeLuca, 2010).
evidence: Inferred from dual-exponential decay fit and supported by citations

claim: In prior studies, the slow-turnover subpopulation has typically been ascribed to the KMTs, while the fast-turnover subpopulation has typically been ascribed to the non-KMTs.
source: In prior studies, the slow-turnover subpopulation has typically been ascribed to the KMTs, while the fast-turnover subpopulation has typically been ascribed to the non-KMTs (Zhai et al., 1995; DeLuca, 2010; Kabeche and Compton, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: The fraction of tubulin in KMTs measured by electron tomography is 25% ± 2% (n=3).
source: We compared the fraction of tubulin in KMTs, 25% ± 2% (n=3), measured by electron tomography (in which a KMT is defined morphologically as a MT with one end associated with a kinetochore; Figure 2F; Kiewisz et al., 2022) to the fraction of the slow-turnover subpopulation measured from photoconversion experiments, 26% ± 2% (n=52).
evidence: Based on analysis of electron tomography data shown in Figure 2F

claim: The fraction of the slow-turnover subpopulation measured from photoconversion experiments is 26% ± 2% (n=52).
source: We compared the fraction of tubulin in KMTs, 25% ± 2% (n=3), measured by electron tomography (in which a KMT is defined morphologically as a MT with one end associated with a kinetochore; Figure 2F; Kiewisz et al., 2022) to the fraction of the slow-turnover subpopulation measured from photoconversion experiments, 26% ± 2% (n=52).
evidence: Based on photoconversion experiments

claim: The fraction of tubulin in KMTs and the fraction of the slow-turnover subpopulation are statistically indistinguishable (p=0.86).
source: Since these two fractions are statistically indistinguishable (Figure 2G, p=0.86 on a Students' t-test), we conclude that the slow-turnover subpopulation are indeed KMTs, and that there is not a significant number of stabilized non-KMTs.
evidence: Based on statistical comparison shown in Figure 2G

claim: The slow-turnover subpopulation are indeed KMTs.
source: Since these two fractions are statistically indistinguishable (Figure 2G, p=0.86 on a Students' t-test), we conclude that the slow-turnover subpopulation are indeed KMTs, and that there is not a significant number of stabilized non-KMTs.
evidence: Inferred from the statistical indistinguishability of the two fractions

claim: There is not a significant number of stabilized non-KMTs.
source: Since these two fractions are statistically indistinguishable (Figure 2G, p=0.86 on a Students' t-test), we conclude that the slow-turnover subpopulation are indeed KMTs, and that there is not a significant number of stabilized non-KMTs.
evidence: Inferred from the statistical indistinguishability of the two fractions

claim: The average speed of the photoconverted lines increased with increasing distance from the pole (Slope = 0.25 ± 0.04(µm/min)/µm, p=4 × 10–8).
source: Combining data from these different spindles revealed that average speed of the photoconverted lines increased with increasing distance from the pole (Figure 3F; Slope = 0.25 ± 0.04(µm/min)/µm, p=4 × 10–8), while both the KMT (Figure 3G; Slope = −0.10 ± 0.15 (1/min)/µm, p=0.50) and non-KMT (Figure 3H; Slope = 0.01 ± 0.01 (1/min)/µm, p=0.13) turnover were independent of distance from the pole.
evidence: Based on analysis of photoconversion data from 52 spindles shown in Figure 3F

claim: KMT turnover is independent of distance from the pole (Slope = −0.10 ± 0.15 (1/min)/µm, p=0.50).
source: Combining data from these different spindles revealed that average speed of the photoconverted lines increased with increasing distance from the pole (Figure 3F; Slope = 0.25 ± 0.04(µm/min)/µm, p=4 × 10–8), while both the KMT (Figure 3G; Slope = −0.10 ± 0.15 (1/min)/µm, p=0.50) and non-KMT (Figure 3H; Slope = 0.01 ± 0.01 (1/min)/µm, p=0.13) turnover were independent of distance from the pole.
evidence: Based on analysis of photoconversion data shown in Figure 3G

claim: Non-KMT turnover is independent of distance from the pole (Slope = 0.01 ± 0.01 (1/min)/µm, p=0.13).
source: Combining data from these different spindles revealed that average speed of the photoconverted lines increased with increasing distance from the pole (Figure 3F; Slope = 0.25 ± 0.04(µm/min)/µm, p=4 × 10–8), while both the KMT (Figure 3G; Slope = −0.10 ± 0.15 (1/min)/µm, p=0.50) and non-KMT (Figure 3H; Slope = 0.01 ± 0.01 (1/min)/µm, p=0.13) turnover were independent of distance from the pole.
evidence: Based on analysis of photoconversion data shown in Figure 3H

claim: Since the non-KMTs turnover roughly every 15–20s, the non-KMT contribution to the motion of the photoconverted line should be negligible roughly 1 minute after photoconversion.
source: Since the non-KMTs turnover roughly every 15–20s, the non-KMT contribution to the motion of the photoconverted line should be negligible roughly 1 minute after photoconversion.
evidence: Inferred from the measured non-KMT turnover rate

claim: The line speed measured is primarily the result of motion of tubulin in KMTs.
source: We typically track the photoconverted line for ~2.5min, so the line speed we measure is primarily the result of motion of tubulin in KMTs.
evidence: Inferred from the rapid turnover of non-KMTs and the tracking duration

claim: The faster line speed further from the pole implies that tubulin in short KMTs, whose minus ends are near the kinetochore, move more quickly than tubulin in long KMTs that reach all the way from the kinetochore to the pole.
source: The faster line speed further from the pole implies that tubulin in short KMTs, whose minus ends are near the kinetochore, move more quickly than tubulin in long KMTs that reach all the way from the kinetochore to the pole.
evidence: Inferred from the spatially varying line speed

claim: The speeds observed with the two-photon photoactivation were very similar to the speeds observed with a traditional one-photon photoactivation system.
source: The speeds we observed with the two-photon photoactivation were very similar to the speeds we observed with a traditional one-photon photoactivation system (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on comparison of two-photon and one-photon photoactivation experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: The measured KMT and non-KMT lifetimes were indistinguishable between the one- and two-photon activation systems (KMT Lifetime: One-Photon: 2.7±0.2min, Two-Photon: 2.8±0.2min, p=0.71; Non-KMT Lifetime: One-Photon: 0.29±0.02min, Two-Photon: 0.26±0.01min, p=0.10).
source: The measured KMT and non-KMT lifetimes were indistinguishable between the one- and two-photon activation systems (KMT Lifetime: One-Photon: 2.7±0.2min, Two-Photon: 2.8±0.2min, p=0.71; Non-KMT Lifetime: One-Photon: 0.29±0.02min, Two-Photon: 0.26±0.01min, p=0.10).
evidence: Based on comparison of one-photon and two-photon photoactivation experiments

claim: The motion of the central portion of the line moved at very similar speeds to the entire line binned together, suggesting that the observed slowdown was not a consequence of increased curvature near the poles.
source: We found that the motion of this central portion of the line moved at very similar speeds to the entire line binned together, suggesting that the observed slowdown was a not a consequence of increased curvature near the poles.
evidence: Based on analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: The speed of the KMTs is faster the further they are from the pole.
source: These results therefore suggest that the speed of the KMTs is faster the further they are from the pole, and that the stability of KMTs and non-KMTs are constant throughout the spindle.
evidence: Based on photoconversion experiments

claim: The stability of KMTs and non-KMTs are constant throughout the spindle.
source: These results therefore suggest that the speed of the KMTs is faster the further they are from the pole, and that the stability of KMTs and non-KMTs are constant throughout the spindle.
evidence: Based on photoconversion experiments

claim: The orientations of non-KMTs and KMTs were very similar to each other throughout the spindle.
source: The orientations of non-KMTs and KMTs were very similar to each other throughout the spindle, as can be seen by comparing the mean orientation of both sets of MTs along the spindle axis (Figure 4D).
evidence: Based on analysis of electron tomography data shown in Figure 4D

claim: The non-KMTs and KMTs align along the same orientation field in the spindle.
source: Thus, the non-KMTs and KMTs align along the same orientation field in the spindle.
evidence: Inferred from the similarity of non-KMT and KMT orientations

claim: The strong alignment of MTs in the spindle along the (spatially varying) average orientation field suggests that MTs in the spindle tend to move and grow along this orientation field.
source: The strong alignment of MTs in the spindle along the (spatially varying) average orientation field suggests that MTs in the spindle tend to move and grow along this orientation field.
evidence: Inferred from the high scalar nematic order parameter

claim: The measured retardance from the PolScope agrees with the predicted retardance from projecting the entire z-depth of the EM reconstructions onto one plane.
source: Consistent with this expectation, the measured retardance from the PolScope agrees with the predicted retardance from projecting the entire z-depth of the EM reconstructions onto one plane (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on comparison shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: The orientation field from LC-Polscope data from eleven HeLa spindles looked remarkably similar to the projected orientations measured by EM.
source: We next averaged together live-cell LC-Polscope data from eleven HeLa spindles and obtained an orientational field (Figure 5B) that looked remarkably similar to the projected orientations measured by EM (compare Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Based on comparison of Figure 5A and Figure 5B

claim: Previous work has shown that an active liquid crystal theory can quantitatively describe the morphology of Xenopus egg extract spindles.
source: Previous work has shown that an active liquid crystal theory can quantitatively describe the morphology of Xenopus egg extract spindles, as well as the statistics of spontaneous fluctuations of MT density, orientations, and stresses in those spindles (Brugués and Needleman, 2014; Oriola et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brugués and Needleman, 2014 and Oriola et al., 2020

claim: Active liquid crystal theories are continuum theories of the collective behaviors of locally interacting, energy consuming molecules that spontaneously align.
source: Active liquid crystal theories are continuum theories of the collective behaviors of locally interacting, energy consuming molecules that spontaneously align (Marchetti et al., 2013; Needleman and Dogic, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Marchetti et al., 2013 and Needleman and Dogic, 2017

claim: The central underlying assumptions in applying active liquid crystal theories to the spindle are that MTs align relative to each other due to their local, mutual interactions, that MTs in the spindle tend to move and grow along the direction defined by their axis, and that the phenomena of interest occur at sufficiently large length-scale such that the continuum approximation is appropriate.
source: The central underlying assumptions in applying these theories to the spindle are that MTs align relative to each other due to their local, mutual interactions, that MTs in the spindle tend to move and grow along the direction defined by their axis, and that the phenomena of interest occur at sufficiently large length-scale such that the continuum approximation is appropriate.
evidence: Describes the assumptions of the theoretical framework

claim: The predicted steady-state orientation of MTs in the spindle is entirely determined by the system geometry and does not explicitly depend on any parameters of the theory.
source: Remarkably, the predicted steady-state orientation of MTs in the spindle is entirely determined by the system geometry – the spindle's boundary and the location of topological defects such as asters near the poles – and does not explicitly depend on any parameters of the theory.
evidence: Property of the Laplace equation solution with specified boundary conditions
